title: Camel Racing and Robot Jockeys
summary: How the old Arabian tradition of camel racing works today, why child jockeys were banned, and how remote-controlled robot jockeys took their place.
poll: Robots are a good way to keep old sports alive.

versions.title: Fast Camels
versions.text:
Have you seen a camel run? It is fast! It can go as fast as a car.

Lots of folks in Saudi Arabia race them. It is an old sport. Long ago, men raced in the sand. It was for fun.

Now there are big race tracks. A track is a long path of sand. The beasts run side by side. The first one to the end wins.

A camel has long legs. Its feet are wide and soft. They do not sink in the sand. So it can run well.

Who rides in a race? The rider is the jockey. Long ago, small boys were the jockeys. They were light. That made the beasts run fast. But it was not safe for the boys. So it had to stop.

Now a robot rides! It is a small box. It sits on the back. It is not big at all.

The man who owns the camel drives a car by the track. He has a remote. He can push it. Then the robot taps the camel. He can talk to it, too. The camel hears him from the box.

This sport mixes old and new. It is fun to watch!

versions.title: Camel Racing and Robot Jockeys
versions.text:
Have you ever watched a camel run at full speed? It is surprisingly fast. In a short sprint, a racing camel can reach about 65 kilometers per hour, as fast as a car on a city street. Camels can also keep up a strong pace over long distances.

Camel racing is an old tradition in Saudi Arabia and other countries of the Arabian Peninsula. Long ago, families raced their camels across the open desert at festivals and weddings. Today, Saudi Arabia holds large camel racing festivals, and the best camels can win their owners big prizes.

Modern races take place on wide sand tracks that are several kilometers long. Most racing camels have one hump, and their bodies suit the desert. They have long legs and wide, padded feet that spread out on soft sand.

For many years, the riders, or jockeys, were young boys, because a light rider helped a camel run faster. But racing was dangerous for children, and they often missed school. In the early 2000s, countries in the region banned child jockeys.

This created a problem: who would ride? The answer was a robot. Qatar first used robot jockeys in 2005. Today, a robot jockey is a small, lightweight machine strapped to the camel's back.

During a race, the owner drives a car along a road beside the track. Using a remote control, he can make the robot tap the camel with a small whip. A speaker on the robot lets the camel hear its owner's voice.

Camel racing shows how a country can keep its old traditions while using new technology.

Most racing camels have a single hump, and their bodies are remarkably adapted to the desert environment, with long legs and broad, padded feet that distribute their weight on soft sand. Trainers customarily exercise them in the cool early morning and pay meticulous attention to their diet and overall health.

For many years, the jockeys were young boys, because a lighter rider helped a camel run faster. However, racing was genuinely dangerous for children, who also frequently missed their education, so in the early 2000s governments throughout the region prohibited child jockeys.

That decision created a practical problem, since every camel still required a rider. The ingenious solution was a robot: Qatar introduced robot jockeys in 2005, and today a robot jockey is a small, lightweight machine strapped securely to the camel's back. The earliest models were heavy and expensive, but engineers steadily improved the design, and contemporary robots weigh only a few kilograms.
